title: VS Code Remote-SSH port forwarding to Framework fails: SELinux sshd_can_network_connect boolean likely off
description:
## Original request (verbatim)

> also /clean-task-panel and lmk why i'm having trouble connecting to my framework machine via
> Remote Explorer extension. it also gave a notification error that it couldn't port forward. idk
> if that's related. do i need the remote explorer or some other extension like remote vs code
> server or something to connect via ssh from macos to framework machine in vs code? whatever it
> is, investigate root cause and /bug-fix or if its more involved, then /delegate to /codex to
> investigate root cause and /bug-fix. also go ahead and create /beads-task and cc task and set
> them to in progress and ship.
>
> [pasted VS Code Remote-SSH connection log ending in:]
> [22:18:35.807] Failed to set up socket for dynamic port forward to remote port 39869: Socket
> closed. TCP port forwarding may be disabled, or the remote server may have crashed.

## Task details

ROOT CAUSE FOUND (not an ai-cli-utils or VS Code bug -- a Framework host SELinux configuration
issue):

Investigated live via direct SSH reproduction. VS Code Remote-SSH extension uses `ssh -D <port>`
(dynamic SOCKS forwarding) to reach the remote VS Code server process on Framework. Reproduced the
exact failure with plain `ssh -v`, and confirmed it affects BOTH dynamic (`-D`) AND static (`-L`)
forwarding identically -- both fail with:

```
channel N: open failed: connect failed: open failed
```

...even against a target port confirmed genuinely listening via `ss -tln` (tested against
127.0.0.1:4222, nats). The extension host's own log
(~/.vscode-server/.<commit>.log on Framework) confirmed the server itself was up and listening
("Server bound to 127.0.0.1:39869 (IPv4)", "Extension host agent started") during the exact
window of the failed connection attempt, then self-terminated 10 minutes later
("ServerLifetime: all consumers inactive, shutting down") because the tunnel never successfully
delivered a client connection to it.

Framework is Fedora with SELinux confirmed Enforcing (`getenforce` -> `Enforcing`,
`sestatus` -> "Current mode: enforcing"). This exact symptom -- sshd authenticates fine, but every
forwarded channel-open fails at the connect step even though the target is genuinely listening --
is the well-documented Fedora/RHEL SELinux signature of the `sshd_can_network_connect` boolean
being off (its default), which blocks sshd from making outbound loopback connections on behalf of
forwarded channels (both -L and -D forwarding go through the same underlying direct-tcpip /
dynamic-tcpip channel-open mechanism, which is why both fail identically).

Could not confirm the exact boolean value or read sshd_config/audit log directly -- both require
root (`getsebool sshd_can_network_connect` failed with "Error getting active value", reading
/etc/ssh/sshd_config and sshd_config.d/ returned Permission denied, `ausearch` needs root). No sudo
password available or attempted.

FIX (requires Sergei's action -- needs root, cannot be done autonomously without his sudo
password):

```
sudo setsebool -P sshd_can_network_connect on
```

(`-P` persists across reboots.) After running this on Framework, retry the VS Code Remote-SSH
connection -- port forwarding (both Remote Explorer's dynamic tunnel and any manual -L/-R forward)
should work.

This is unrelated to the mosh/AI-CLI-e2nv work from earlier this cycle -- confirmed via direct
side-by-side testing that mosh's own SSH-based bootstrap to Framework (via the `fw` config alias,
same host) works fine for the actual remote command execution; only forwarded/tunneled port
connections are affected, which mosh doesn't use.

Does the user need a different/additional extension (e.g. a dedicated "Remote - Tunnels" or
different remote server)? No -- Remote-SSH is the correct extension for this workflow; nothing
else is needed once the SELinux boolean is fixed.
notes: Reopened per Sergei: VS Code Remote-SSH dynamic port forwarding to Framework still failing live (fresh log confirms same 'channel N: open failed: connect failed: open failed' symptom, 2026-09-01 02:34-02:39). Code-side diagnostic fix shipped (ai-cli-utils@7d1ae22) and root cause/remedy documented (docs/bugs/selinux-sshd-session-port-forwarding.md), but the actual unblocking action -- running audit2allow/semodule as root on Framework -- has not been confirmed done yet. Keep open/in_progress until Sergei confirms the VS Code connection actually works.
close_reason: Confirmed fixed by Sergei: ran the SELinux remedy on Framework (sudo ausearch | audit2allow -M sshd_session_local && sudo semodule -i sshd_session_local.pp), VS Code Remote-SSH now connects successfully. Root cause + remedy documented (docs/bugs/selinux-sshd-session-port-forwarding.md), code-side diagnostic fix shipped (ai-cli-utils@7d1ae22).

title: mosh's terminal-restore erases real remote error text before "[mosh is exiting.]", masking every fast remote-command failure
description:
## Original request (verbatim)

> Why you never saw this text: mosh clears/restores the terminal after the remote command exits
> and before printing "[mosh is exiting.]" — the exact same masking behavior already documented
> in the code as AI-CLI-gg9s.
>
> Address this issue. If not, then create a CC task for this and set the /beads-task and CC task
> to in progress, ship those changes, and then /delegate to /codex to investigate the Root cause
> and /bug-fix.

## Task details

Confirmed live while root-causing AI-CLI-sgqy (closed): when the remote command launched over
mosh (src/ai_cli/main.py's `remote_cmd`, run via `mosh_args` in transport.py's
`_run_transport_loop`) fails fast for ANY reason, mosh's own terminal-restore erases the real
remote stderr/stdout before printing "[mosh is exiting.]" -- the user only ever sees
transport.py's generic "Transport exited too quickly ({elapsed:.1f}s) — giving up." (line 353),
never the actual error. This is the same masking pattern already documented in
`_resolve_remote_shell`'s docstring (main.py:1257-1265, referencing "AI-CLI-gg9s") for the shell
probe specifically -- but the masking applies to EVERY remote-command failure under mosh, not
just a missing shell, and there is no general fix for it.

Concretely: in this cycle's sw-4 investigation, the real cause (a stale, unregistered
.worktrees/sw-4 directory refusing worktree creation -- session.py:1133-1160's deliberate safety
guard) was completely invisible to Sergei. He saw only "Transport exited too quickly" three times
in a row with zero diagnostic content, and it took a manual plain-SSH reproduction (bypassing
mosh) to surface the real "create_worktree: ... refusing to delete it" error text.

Fix direction (needs careful design, not a quick patch): in `_run_transport_loop`'s
`elapsed < 3` mosh fast-fail branch (transport.py ~line 351), before giving up, surface the real
remote error to the user. The naive approach -- just re-running the same `remote_cmd` over a
captured (non-pty) SSH connection as a "diagnostic" -- has a real side-effect risk: if the
original failure was transient, the diagnostic re-run could itself succeed and silently launch a
second live CC session as an unintended side effect of what's meant to be read-only diagnostics.
A safe fix likely needs either: (a) a dedicated read-only/dry-run probe flag on the remote-side
`ai c ... --is-remote` invocation that reports what would happen without actually launching
anything, or (b) have the remote_cmd tee its own stderr to a local state file during the real
attempt (not a second re-run) and have the transport loop read+print that file's tail after mosh
exits fast, with no re-execution risk at all. Prefer (b) if tractable -- it reports the real
failure from the real attempt, not a second attempt's possibly-different outcome.

Investigate root cause end-to-end (confirm the exact masking mechanism, e.g. via `mosh --ssh`
option internals or strace if needed) and implement a fix using approach (b) if practical,
falling back to (a) with explicit safeguards against a duplicate live launch if not. Include
regression test coverage. Set to in_progress immediately, ship the .beads export, then delegate
to Codex for implementation.
close_reason: Fixed and shipped (7a45a72, Codex-authored, independently RED/GREEN verified). Real mosh remote command now tees its own stderr to a unique per-launch state file during its one real attempt; the transport loop reads it back via a read-only, non-interactive SSH command (test/tail/rm only, no re-execution) when mosh exits fast, so the real remote error is now surfaced instead of a generic 'Transport exited too quickly' message. Deployed to all 3 install locations (Mac, Hetzner, Framework) + aido venv.

title: test_stale_session_reaper.py's bash/zsh supervisor tests fail under xdist parallelism even with zero leaked processes present
description:
## Original request (verbatim)

Not a direct user request - split out from AI-CLI-1xg0 while shipping its fixture-teardown fix, per "fix what you find" / never leave a loose thread only in chat.

## Task details

AI-CLI-1xg0's fixture-teardown fix (shipped, commit 7db83f5) closed the leaked-process problem but did NOT resolve the underlying flake in tests/test_stale_session_reaper.py's bash/zsh-parametrized supervisor tests ("supervisor child did not become ready", 14/20 failing).

Measured this session, with zero leaked processes present on a clean machine:
- `uv run pytest tests/test_stale_session_reaper.py -q -n 0` (serial, no xdist): all tests pass reliably, comfortably under the 15s readiness deadline.
- `uv run pytest tests/test_stale_session_reaper.py -q` (default `-n auto` xdist): the same 14 tests fail every time with "supervisor child did not become ready", reproduced 3 separate times.
- Tried bumping `_wait_for_path`'s deadline from 15s to 45s as a quick mitigation: did NOT fix it -- the failing tests just took longer (136s vs 46s wall time) before still failing the same way. Reverted since it added latency with no benefit.

This points at genuine xdist worker contention (many parallel workers each spawning real bash/zsh subprocesses simultaneously) rather than a fixed/slow readiness check. Needs investigation:
- Is this specific to this Mac's current load/core count, or does it reproduce elsewhere?
- Could this file's supervisor tests be forced onto reduced parallelism (e.g. `pytest-xdist`'s `--dist loadgroup` + `@pytest.mark.xdist_group`) so they don't all fire at once, without serializing the whole suite?
- Is something about the fake `ps`/`tmux`/`ai` shell-script stand-ins or `portalocker` file locking under `tmp_path` genuinely contended (not just CPU-starved) under concurrent workers?

Not fixed in this pass -- out of proportion for a same-session follow-on to AI-CLI-1xg0 (would need real experimentation with xdist config, not a one-line change).
notes: New evidence 2026-08-30 while independently verifying a separate Codex delegation (AI-CLI-t8h5 round 2): the same 14-test failure set (supervisor child did not become ready) reproduces even with -n 0 (serial execution, no xdist), contradicting the "xdist-parallelism contention" framing from the prior cycle. Confirmed pre-existing (same signature observed earlier this session, unrelated worktree, before any of today's fixes). Possibly related to the SIGTTOU background-process-group issue just fixed for AI-CLI-t8h5 (session_script.py's _supervisor_restore_terminal), but NOT resolved by that fix -- ran the full test_stale_session_reaper.py suite WITH the SIGTTOU fix applied and still got the same 14 failures. Worth investigating whether many real-tmux-server tests running sequentially in one pytest process leave residual terminal/process-group state that contaminates later tests, rather than a pure xdist-scheduling race.
close_reason: Same root cause as AI-CLI-1xg0 (stale inherited supervisor file descriptors), now fixed there (6915110). The xdist-contention framing was a red herring from an earlier diagnosis pass -- confirmed the fix resolves the flake even in fully serial runs (-n 0).

title: test_stale_session_reaper.py: 14 tests fail with 'supervisor child did not become ready' (pre-existing, not xdist-only)
description:
Found while verifying AI-CLI-p3fg's fix was RED-before/GREEN-after via a
targeted git-stash comparison against the unmodified base commit
(origin/main, 525b6f3). Not caused by that change: same 14 failures
reproduce identically with the AI-CLI-p3fg diff fully stashed out.

All 14 failures are in tests/test_stale_session_reaper.py, every one
failing with the identical message "supervisor child did not become ready"
(both bash and zsh parametrizations of most cases). This is a subprocess
supervisor readiness race - the test spawns a generated supervisor script
and polls (20ms interval) for a "ready" signal from its child before a
timeout, and that readiness never arrives in time on this run.

Full suite run: 14 failed, 2510 passed, 17 skipped (~126s), macOS. Isolated
re-run of just this file: 14 failed, 16 passed, 4 skipped (~52s) - same set
fails whether run as part of the full suite or in isolation, so it is not
purely an xdist parallel-load artifact, though this Mac was also running
several other CC background processes at the time (see AI-CLI-p3fg for
that unrelated investigation) which may still be a contributing factor to
timing pressure.

Needs proper root-cause: is this a genuine race in the supervisor script's
own readiness-signaling logic, a test-harness polling/timeout issue, or
purely host-load-dependent flakiness? Not fixed here - out of proportion
for the AI-CLI-p3fg session (~30+ min root-cause estimate), filed per
"fix what you find" instead.
notes: ESCALATION 2026-08-31: this flake was just observed reproducing 100% of the time (3/3 serial attempts, -n 0, on an UNTOUCHED pre-existing test unrelated to any change), not just intermittently as previously tracked. Blocked independent verification of AI-CLI-56br's fix (had to fall back to an isolated bash+zsh logic test instead of the real pytest harness). Worth prioritizing given it now appears to have gotten worse, not better.
close_reason: Root-caused (Codex-authored, independently verified) and fixed (6915110): a new supervisor inheriting stale AI_CLI_SUPERVISOR_LEASE_FD/TERMINAL_FD/CHILD_READY_PATH from an earlier unrelated session used those invalid descriptors and crashed with OSError Bad file descriptor before writing its ready marker -- a real product bug, not a test flake. Fixed by unsetting those supervisor-only vars before establishing a new supervisor's own state. Independently verified against the ORIGINAL unmodified test fixture: 34 passed/6 skipped/0 failed. Full repo suite: 2550 passed, 18 skipped, 0 failed (was 14 failing before).

title: Copy-on-selection to system clipboard for tmux sessions (incl. remote/Pi), without holding Option
description:
User request (2026-08-29): currently, copying text from a tmux pane launched by this tool (ai c ...) requires holding Option to force iTerm2's native mouse selection/copy, bypassing tmux. User wants plain mouse-drag selection to copy straight to the system clipboard, no modifier key, including for Pi CLI sessions specifically.

User supplied a Google AI summary suggesting: enable tmux mouse mode + bind copy-mode selection to pipe through macOS's `pbcopy`. That answer is INCOMPLETE for this tool and will not work as-is for its main use case:

- `pbcopy` only exists on macOS. This tool's primary differentiator is launching sessions on REMOTE Linux hosts over SSH (Hetzner, Framework -- see [remote.machines.*] in config.toml) via `ai c -R -m <alias>`. A tmux config that pipes to `pbcopy` works for a LOCAL session but does nothing (or errors) for a remote one, since there is no pbcopy binary on the remote host.
- The correct cross-platform mechanism for this tool's shape is tmux's OSC 52 clipboard passthrough (`set -s set-clipboard on`, tmux >= 3.2), which makes tmux emit an OSC 52 escape sequence on copy that travels back up through the SSH connection to the LOCAL terminal (iTerm2), which writes it to the system clipboard -- this works identically for local and remote sessions, and does not require any clipboard binary on the remote host at all.
- iTerm2 has its own gate for this: Preferences > General > 'Applications in terminal may access clipboard' must be enabled. That's a one-time host-side iTerm2 app preference this CLI tool cannot set programmatically -- needs to be documented as a manual one-time step for the user.
- Enabling `set -g mouse on` changes tmux's mouse handling globally for that session (click-drag enters copy-mode instead of native terminal selection; scroll wheel behavior also changes). Needs to be verified this doesn't conflict with anything Pi CLI sessions specifically rely on (see related AI-CLI-unj3 / AI-CLI-support-pi-cli-sessions-iterm2-djaa, currently open, about Pi + iTerm2 integration -- tab title/icon/pane formatting; this is a different but adjacent concern, may share investigation).
- tmux version matters: OSC52 passthrough via `set-clipboard` has evolved across tmux 2.x/3.x; needs verification against whatever tmux version is actually installed on hz (Hetzner) and fw (Framework) remotes, not just this Mac's local tmux 3.7c.

Where in the codebase this likely belongs: src/ai_cli/session_script.py's get_engine_script() already sets tmux session options at launch time (e.g. remain-on-exit, per AI-CLI-tdm6.1) -- this would be another such option, added to that same code path, ideally gated so it doesn't silently change behavior for local-only usage.

Needs research + implementation. Delegating investigation of the exact correct tmux config (mouse + set-clipboard + any copy-mode key rebinding needed) to Codex rather than trusting the incomplete Google AI summary; Codex should verify tmux version behavior differences and confirm the OSC52 remote-passthrough approach is right before implementing.

title: test_stale_session_reaper.py: pass_fds not supported on Windows
description:
tests/test_stale_session_reaper.py::test_given_shell_held_descriptor_when_python_lock_helper_exits_then_lease_remains_held
fails on Windows CI with: AssertionError: pass_fds not supported on Windows.

subprocess.Popen's pass_fds parameter is POSIX-only (raises ValueError on Windows
per the stdlib docs). This test (and likely the underlying lease/lock-descriptor
mechanism in stale_session_reaper.py or session_script.py it exercises, added as
part of AD-5's job-control/portalocker work, commits 8a25e04/268970b) uses
pass_fds to hand a held file descriptor to a child process for a lock test.

Needs either: (a) an explicit skip for this test on Windows if the underlying
mechanism is genuinely POSIX-only and Windows uses a different lock path
(portalocker is meant to be cross-platform -- check whether this specific test
is exercising a POSIX-only code path that Windows doesn't take in production,
in which case skip is correct), or (b) a cross-platform equivalent using
STARTUPINFO/handle inheritance if the underlying behavior needs to be verified
on Windows too.

title: Remote mosh CC sessions on framework lost native clipboard copy-on-selection, falling back to tmux internal buffer

comments.author: Sergei Wallace
comments.text:
## Symptom

Sergei's mac-hosted CC sessions launched onto framework-fedora via `ai c {index} -R -m fw`
(mosh + tmux) now show, on native copy-on-selection:

```
copied 79 chars to tmux buffer · paste with prefix + ]
```

instead of the expected

```
copied 243 chars to clipboard
```

The latter is what a non-remote, non-tmux CC session (`ai-cli-1`) still shows, and what the
remote framework sessions themselves used to show before something changed ("this was working
before, what changed?" -- Sergei, 2026-08-29).

## Working hypothesis (not yet confirmed)

On the framework-fedora side, inside tmux:

```
$ env | grep -E 'TERM_PROGRAM|TMUX|SSH_TTY'
TERM_PROGRAM=tmux
TMUX=/tmp/tmux-1000/default,...
SSH_TTY=/dev/pts/4
```

`TERM_PROGRAM=tmux` is tmux's own override of whatever the outer terminal originally reported.
Claude Code's copy-on-selection feature likely branches on `TERM_PROGRAM` (or an equivalent
signal) to decide whether to emit a real OSC 52 clipboard escape vs. fall back to tmux's internal
buffer -- and `tmux` is exactly the value that would make it choose the conservative fallback,
regardless of whether tmux itself would actually relay OSC 52 through (this box's tmux already has
`set-clipboard external` and `terminal-features` includes `xterm*:clipboard`, so relaying should
work if CC tried it).

This is a **hypothesis worth verifying, not a confirmed root cause.** It does not yet explain the
regression (why this SPECIFIC framework+mosh+tmux combination used to work and stopped) --
possible explanations to check:

1. A Claude Code CLI version bump changed its OSC 52 / tmux-detection heuristic.
2. A local tmux config change (`~/.tmux.conf`, last modified 2026-08-25) altered `set-clipboard`,
   `terminal-features`, or `terminal-overrides` in a way that changed CC's detection (even though
   the current values look correct on inspection).
3. A mosh version change altered what TERM/TERM_PROGRAM it negotiates/passes through.
4. Something in `ai-cli-utils`' `ai c ... -R -m fw` launch path changed how it invokes
   tmux/mosh/ssh for a remote framework session specifically (vs. a local session like `ai-cli-1`).

## Investigation requested

1. Confirm or refute the `TERM_PROGRAM` hypothesis: compare the full environment (`env`) of a
   currently-broken framework+mosh+tmux CC session against a currently-working local session
   (`ai-cli-1`), focusing on `TERM_PROGRAM`, `TERM`, `TMUX`, `COLORTERM`, `SSH_TTY`,
   `MOSH_CONNECT`/similar.
2. Check `git log -p -- ~/.tmux.conf` isn't applicable (untracked dotfile) -- instead check
   `ai-cli-utils`' own git history for any recent change to how `ai c -R -m fw` launches a remote
   session (tmux invocation flags, `TERM`/`TERM_PROGRAM` env passthrough, mosh invocation).
3. Check whether Claude Code has a recently-changed or documented OSC 52/clipboard detection
   heuristic (release notes, `claude-code-guide` agent, or public docs) that explains branching on
   `TERM_PROGRAM=tmux`.
4. **If the root cause is confirmed to be Claude Code's own internal detection logic (not
   something in `ai-cli-utils` or this session's tmux config)**, this is NOT fixable by a patch in
   our repos -- say so explicitly rather than forcing a workaround, and recommend `/report-feedback`
   to Anthropic with the reproduction. If it IS something `ai-cli-utils`' launcher controls (e.g. it
   should be preserving/forwarding the original terminal's `TERM_PROGRAM` through mosh+tmux rather
   than letting tmux's own override win), fix it there with a regression test.

comments.author: Sergei Wallace
comments.text:
Root-caused: Claude Code 2.1.251's own native/tmux/OSC52 classifier maps any non-native tmux session to "tmux-buffer" regardless of actual clipboard delivery success; ai-cli-utils's launcher creates the tmux+mosh topology but does not own the classification or toast text. No repository fix warranted -- recommends /report-feedback to Anthropic.

title: Expose typed exit codes distinguishing config/prereq vs transient vs partial-mutation causes in cc_usage.py, quota.py, and copier_update.py
description:
Originating decision: ai-core CORE-201/AD-3 (2026-08-26, Sergei approved option (a) for
cross-repo scope, via chat with the kc-1 session). ai-core's scheduler treats these three wrappers'
non-zero exits as one generic retry-policy class, but ground-truthed causes differ:

- cc_usage.py: missing usage_api URL/key (deterministic, don't retry) vs a transport/network
  failure (retry).
- quota.py: missing tmux/Claude, an incompatible /usage contract, or invalid remote configuration
  (deterministic) vs a timeout/SSH failure (retry).
- copier_update.py: missing projects root/copier binary or a pre-mutation configuration/service
  failure (deterministic) vs a recorded post-mutation conflict/push/update partial effect (needs
  its own recovery disposition, not a blanket terminal).

Ask: expose distinct, documented exit codes (or another typed signal ai-core's handler can read)
for at minimum: (1) missing prerequisite/config (deterministic, don't retry as transient), (2)
transient I/O failure (retry), (3) for copier_update specifically, a partial-mutation-completed
signal distinct from a clean pre-mutation failure. Full ground-truthing and verification commands
are in ai-core's docs/audits/core-201-scheduling-reliability-remediation-plan-audit.md and
docs/plans/core-201-scheduling-reliability-remediation-plan.md:635 (cross-repo contract table).

Filed by kc-1 immediately after repairing this repo's local Beads Dolt store (AIH-mvipu /
AIH-ai-cli-utils-local-beads-dolt-pvvg), which was the blocker preventing this filing.
close_reason: Implemented via Codex (gpt-5.6-terra, codex/implement --effort high), independently verified by kc-1 (diff-by-diff review, full test suite re-run: 241 passed matching self-report, 19 pre-existing unrelated failures confirmed pre-existing against unmodified origin/main). cc_usage.py/quota.py distinguish exit 78 (config/prereq) from 75 (transient); copier_update.py additionally gets exit 3 (EX_PARTIAL_MUTATION) for the conflict/pushfail partial-mutation-completed case, taking precedence over config/transient per the issue's ask. Landed main (71cda64).

title: Flaky test: detached_ticker_continues_ticking[bash] times out ~1-in-5 under full-file xdist parallel load
description:
## Original request (verbatim)

Not directly requested -- discovered while independently verifying AD-5's follow-up fix (AI-CLI-9s2k).

## Task details

tests/test_stale_session_reaper.py::test_given_child_sharing_foreground_process_group_when_terminal_signal_arrives_then_detached_ticker_continues_ticking[bash] genuinely passes when run alone or with a small subset (confirmed 4 separate isolated runs, always PASSED), but fails via subprocess.TimeoutExpired (5s) in roughly 1 of 5 full-file runs (uv run pytest -q tests/test_stale_session_reaper.py, 21 items, 8-way xdist parallelism on this Mac). Always the same single test, always bash flavor, always a timeout not an assertion failure -- consistent with a timing-margin issue under CPU contention (the detached heartbeat ticker's tick interval and/or the test's polling deadline being too tight when 7-8 other real-subprocess tests are competing for CPU), not a logic defect in the shipped fix.

Fix direction: widen the test's polling deadline and/or the fast_heartbeat interval used in this test, or reduce xdist worker count for this specific test module, so the assertion has enough real-world slack under parallel load. Do not touch the underlying supervisor implementation for this -- the property itself (ticker keeps ticking through a terminal signal reaching the foreground child) is confirmed correct by every isolated run.

title: Redesign naming convention for tmux sessions, worktrees, and session names -- client type, remote/transport, machine alias, repo alias
description:
## Original request (verbatim)

Also, one thing I'm thinking about now is I think we need to change the conventions for our Tmux processes, the naming conventions for our Tmux processes and our work trees and our session names, our like Claude and Pi session names and stuff. I think we need to have it include the following information in like some standardized convention. You know, it should include whether it's - I guess the Tmux session name seems to already include some of this. it already includes whether it's pi or claude or codex or gemini and also if it's the team mix process name if it's codexed is it set the prefix to cx if not it should but also what we need to include is which machine it's on so it needs to use like the one or two letter machine abbreviation and we can come up with those for all my machines or it can be i guess that may be up to three letters too. I can list those out kind of what I want but we need to in a standardized format we need to include what type of session it is like the CLI client so if it's quad code or pi or gemini or codex or whatever and it can support future ones as well ... back to the naming conventions I wanted to, like the branch should the worktree should The Tmux process name should include first, like the letter or letters for what AI session client it is, like Pi or codex or claude code or Gemini or whatever. And it can support future ones in a configurable systematic approach. so maybe we have like a shared foundation like a shared like underlying library or framework or whatever and then we can have adapters for different clients or however that works with inheritance and object oriented programming and abstraction and you know whatever framework and library approach with adapters and all that stuff, whatever makes sense, best practice system design and all that. And then the second, like after a hyphen, the second one should be the r letter or like it should be the optional like whether it's remote or local session like if it's remote whether it's like you know it's ssh or mosh or whatever being connected to another machine and then also the next one is not optional it's after like another hyphen it's the machine the machine name or the machine like alias like a short alias for our machine. So like I have my Mac OS machine, I have my framework machine, I have my Accenture Windows machine. I'm going to eventually soon in a couple weeks, I'm going to have like an Accenture MacBook Air. And also I have my BMS SageMaker machine, I have my BMS Windows machine. So we need to have short aliases for all these. So we can come up with like an alias mapping table or whatever for the machines and it should be I think at most three letters but ideally one or two letters. but we can figure that out. And then after that hyphen, then it's the repo that it's launched from, the alias for that. And then after that, it's either the numeric prefix or if I have an optional tag I want to add, then I can do that. And then it can be like an index after that maybe. So we need to figure out this system, and then maybe we'll delegate to Opus to either update. If we don't have a /doc --kind design for all this stuff, we should. So we can delegate to Opus to update or write the /doc --kind design and use the /decision-framework to make any decisions. And then we'll delegate to codex to /auto-flow this. But let's first align on kind of high-level requirements and what I want, and any details like the Tmux process naming conventions and WorkTree naming conventions and machine alias mapping tables and whatever else for all these conventions. So create /beads-task(s) and cc tasks for all this stuff, and we'll follow up on this.

Also, for work trees specifically: we don't need to include remote (the R letter is in the tmux
process name), but we should include the machine always, because worktrees get pushed to remote
for sessions and we need to know which machine a worktree came from.

## Task details (extracted requirements, for a future /doc --kind design pass)

Proposed segment order (client-first, tmux process/session name):
1. Client-type letter(s) -- claude, pi, codex, gemini, extensible to future clients. Codex sessions
   should use prefix "cx" (currently inconsistent per Sergei's observation -- audit current state).
2. Optional remote/transport marker -- whether the session is local or remote, and if remote,
   which transport (ssh/mosh/etc).
3. Machine alias (required, 1-3 letters, ideally 1-2) -- needs an alias mapping table covering:
   macOS (primary Mac), Framework Desktop, Accenture Windows, an upcoming Accenture MacBook Air,
   BMS SageMaker, BMS Windows. Sergei will supply/confirm the actual short aliases.
4. Repo alias.
5. Numeric prefix and/or an optional free-form tag, then an optional index.

Worktree naming: same convention but WITHOUT the remote/transport segment (worktrees aren't
inherently remote/local the way a live tmux process is) -- but the machine alias should ALWAYS be
included for worktrees too, since worktrees get pushed to remote machines for cross-session work
and provenance needs to be traceable.

Architecture ask: a shared foundation/library with adapters per CLI client (Claude/Pi/Codex/Gemini/
future), object-oriented or otherwise -- "whatever makes sense, best practice system design."

Sergei's explicit process: (1) align on high-level requirements first (this issue is that
alignment-tracking step -- do NOT implement yet), (2) delegate to Opus to write/update a
docs/designs/*.md via /doc --kind design, using /decision-framework for any open decisions
(e.g. exact alias table, exact separator/segment grammar), (3) delegate to codex /auto-flow for
implementation once the design is approved.

Related: AI-CLI-l5t (Typer CLI migration, DESIGN-FIRST) may intersect with a client-adapter
architecture -- check for overlap when scoping the design doc. Also intersects with the new Pi
iTerm2 support task and the VS Code terminal customization follow-up task (both filed alongside
this one) -- all three should probably be read together when scoping the design.

title: test_process_probe SIGCONT/SIGKILL fallback test crashes via psutil internals
description:
## Original request (verbatim)

> Discovered during AI-CLI-tdm6's Phase 1 implement-stage full-suite pytest run, 2026-08-28. Confirmed pre-existing on main (HEAD a6fec7a) before the stale-session-reaper Phase 1 diff landed -- process_probe.py's end_process() method itself was not touched by that diff (only capture_identity() was added nearby).

## Task details

tests/test_process_probe.py::test_given_no_sigkill_or_sigcont_when_a_process_is_ended_then_it_still_ends
fails with AttributeError: module 'signal' has no attribute 'SIGCONT' (and separately 'SIGKILL').

The test monkeypatches signal.SIGKILL/signal.SIGCONT away (delattr) to simulate a platform lacking
those constants, then calls PsutilProbe().end_process(pid). end_process() delegates to
psutil.Process.resume(), which internally does "if POSIX: self._send_signal(signal.SIGCONT)"
unconditionally -- psutil's own code crashes when the attribute is missing, rather than our
end_process() wrapper handling the AttributeError gracefully.

Needs root-cause: either end_process() should catch AttributeError around the psutil calls it makes
(since this design's whole safety model requires fail-closed/preserve-on-error behavior for process
operations -- this is directly relevant to the stale-session-reaper's process-identity capture path),
or the test's premise (simulating a platform without these signal constants) needs revisiting since
real Unix platforms always have SIGCONT/SIGKILL and this may be testing an unreachable case.

Reproduce: uv run pytest tests/test_process_probe.py::test_given_no_sigkill_or_sigcont_when_a_process_is_ended_then_it_still_ends -q
close_reason: Duplicate of AI-CLI-t4aq (same test, same root cause, same fix direction).

title: Restore stale-tmux-session cleanup with real CC-process liveness detection, not just pane idle/attach timeout
description:
## Original request (verbatim)

> But do we want this feature in some form? I think it makes sense to keep it for stuff like when I use Termius iOS app to connect to sessions and then they end up being stale or whatever the case may be. But I think it's just not working correctly and it's killing CC sessions that are live. So I think we just need to figure out how to do it properly and detect when a CC session is actually active and live inside a Tmux process.

## Task details

Follow-up to AI-CLI-p2qj (P0, fixed in a223fe5): that fix REMOVED cleanup_stale_sessions()'s
cross-session tmux kill-session entirely, because it was killing unrelated live sessions (timing-
dependent -- whichever siblings happened to cross a detached/aged threshold at the moment of a
DIFFERENT session's launch). That removal was intentionally blunt: get the dangerous behavior gone
first, not ship a cleverer version of the same bug under time pressure.

Sergei wants the cleanup restored in a form that only ever kills a session whose CC process is
PROVABLY dead/gone -- never one that's merely detached (e.g. a Termius iOS client disconnected from
tmux while the remote CC process is still very much alive and running).

Design direction: reuse process_probe.py's already-proven-safe liveness/identity primitives (used
by main.py's _reclaim_abandoned_cc_session and _cc_session_is_live, which is explicitly scoped to
the resuming session only and has never been implicated in a cross-session kill). Apply the SAME
kind of positive-proof-of-death check per tmux pane -- map each pane's leading process to a PID,
and only reap it if process_probe confirms that specific process is gone/zombie -- rather than the
removed code's 'pane idle for N minutes + no attached client' heuristic, which cannot distinguish
a legitimately-disconnected-but-still-running remote session from a genuinely abandoned one.

## Acceptance criteria

- A stale/orphaned tmux session (CC process provably dead, e.g. crashed or exited without cleaning
  up its own pane) is still reaped automatically on a future launch.
- A tmux session with a live, still-running CC process is NEVER killed, regardless of attach state,
  idle time, or which session's launch triggered the cleanup pass (a disconnected Termius client
  must not make its session look 'abandoned').
- Regression test: a live-but-detached session (simulating a Termius disconnect) survives a cleanup
  pass triggered by a DIFFERENT session's launch.
- Regression test: a genuinely dead session (process confirmed gone) IS reaped.
- Full test suite green, ruff clean.
notes: Delegated to Codex implement (balanced/gpt-5.6-terra/medium), isolated worktree, background task b7wjhumdo -- 2026-08-27. Confirmed before delegating: the removed heuristic never used process_probe.py at all (it judged staleness from tmux attach-state metadata only); process_probe.py's liveness primitives are a separate, already-safe mechanism used by _reclaim_abandoned_cc_session, never implicated in the cross-session kill bug.
close_reason: Shipped 549abe9: cleanup_stale_sessions() now reaps via process_probe liveness (all panes ended), fail-closed on unreadable PID. Full test_session.py: 137 passed except 1 pre-existing unrelated direnv/worktree failure (confirmed pre-existing at prior HEAD via stash test). ruff clean.

title: Pre-existing test failures: signal.SIGCONT/SIGKILL AttributeError and direnv-allow-ordering assertion
description:

title: Enable Shift+Enter newline in remote Framework CC sessions (tmux extended-keys)
description:
## Original request (verbatim)

> also, add a /beads-task and cc task to enable me to use shift+enter to do new lines on my
> remote host framework cc sessions from this iterm2 terminal. I think we may just need to
> change the default terminal to warp or another one that supports shift + enter, right? i
> think the default fedora linux terminal doesn't support it, right? can you ssh and do all
> that for me. set that cc task to in progress and then do that

## Task details

**The Fedora default-terminal hypothesis was wrong** -- corrected with evidence below. These are
headless CLI sessions over SSH/mosh from iTerm2; no GUI terminal app on Framework's own display
is ever in the loop, so swapping it for Warp/anything else would have done nothing. (Framework
does already have warp-terminal installed, for what it's worth -- irrelevant here either way.)

### Actual root cause (confirmed via config inspection, 2026-08-25)

iTerm2's Default profile already has the correct Shift-Return key mapping
(`0xd-0x20000-0x24` -> Action 10 (send escape sequence) -> text `[27;2;13~`, i.e. the standard
xterm extended-key-reporting sequence `ESC[27;2;13~` for Shift+Return). This is a static
"send text" mapping, so it fires identically for local and remote (SSH/mosh) sessions --
iTerm2 intercepts the physical keypress before any transport is involved.

`ai c -R -m fw` sessions run inside **tmux** on the remote host (`c-r-<name>` sessions, confirmed
live: aih-1, aih-2, job-1, kc-1, sw-4 all running under `tmux 3.7b` on Framework). tmux has its
own key-input layer that must be told to pass "extended" (modifier-bearing) key sequences like
Shift+Enter's `ESC[27;2;13~` through to the program running in the pane -- controlled by tmux's
`extended-keys` option (tmux 3.2+), off by default.

**The Mac already has this solved**: `~/.tmux.conf` on this machine contains (with a comment
naming this exact scenario):
```
# Pass extended keys (Shift+Enter, etc.) through to applications like Claude Code
set -s extended-keys on
set -as terminal-features 'xterm*:extkeys'
```
**Framework had no `~/.tmux.conf` at all** (`cat: /home/sergeiwallace/.tmux.conf: No such file or
directory`, confirmed via ssh) -- so its tmux ran on bare defaults, `extended-keys off`, silently
downgrading every Shift+Enter to a plain Enter for every remote CC session. This tmux config file
was simply never propagated from Mac to Framework.

### Fix applied this session

1. `scp ~/.tmux.conf fw:~/.tmux.conf` -- copied the Mac's tmux config to Framework verbatim.
2. `ssh fw 'tmux source-file ~/.tmux.conf'` -- reloaded the LIVE tmux server on Framework so the
   fix applies immediately to all 5 already-running remote sessions (aih-1, aih-2, job-1, kc-1,
   sw-4), not just future ones.
3. Verified via `tmux show-options -g extended-keys` -> `on` and
   `tmux show-options -g terminal-features` -> includes `xterm*:extkeys`, both now matching the
   Mac's config exactly.
4. Config file now persists on Framework's disk, so future tmux server (re)starts pick it up
   automatically -- this is not a one-time live-server patch that will regress on reboot.

### Still needs (the one thing I can't verify headlessly)

A human keypress confirmation: press Shift+Enter in an already-running remote Framework CC
session (e.g. reattach to `c-r-sw-4` or any of the 5 listed above) and confirm it inserts a
newline instead of submitting. The config-level fix is applied and verified server-side; only the
actual keystroke-to-render behavior needs eyes-on confirmation, which I can't do as a headless
agent.

### Follow-up worth considering (not done this session, flagging only)

Framework's `~/.tmux.conf` is now a one-time copy, not a managed/synced file -- if the Mac's
tmux config changes in the future, Framework won't pick it up automatically unless something
(the ai sync tooling, or a dotfiles-sync mechanism) keeps it current. Whether that's worth
automating is a separate call; not scoping it into this issue.
close_reason: User confirmed live: Shift+Enter inserts a newline in remote Framework CC sessions. tmux extended-keys fix (this session's manual patch, then durably shipped via ai-harness install.sh AIH-nbd3k) works as intended.

title: Add `ai ssh <machine>` command to shell-connect to configured remote hosts
description:
## Original request (verbatim)

> can you create a remote ssh alias like we have for hetzner but for framework machine. and in
> fact, if we can just have an ai-cli-utils `ai` command to ssh connect to my remote hosts, then
> do that. if we don't already have that, then add a /beads-task and cc task for that and set to
> in progress and then /delegate to /codex to /implement. also, give me command to ssh connect to
> framework right now in the short term while that is done.

## Task details

Add a generic `ai ssh [MACHINE]` command to ai-cli-utils that opens a plain interactive SSH shell
to a remote host configured under `[remote.machines.<alias>]` in config.toml (the same table
`ai c -R -m <alias>` already reads for host/user/port/identity_file). Confirmed via grep of
src/ai_cli/main.py (2026-08-25) that no such generic connect command exists today — only
`ai c -R -m <alias>` (launches a full CC/Gemini session over mosh/ssh), `ai tunnel
start/stop/status` (autossh tunnels), `ai reconnect` (prints reconnect commands for existing
remote tmux CC sessions), and one hardcoded `ai handoff post --remote` ssh call. None of these is
"just SSH me into a configured host."

### Acceptance criteria

- `ai ssh <alias>` (e.g. `ai ssh fw`, `ai ssh hz`) execs an interactive `ssh` session to the host
  configured under `[remote.machines.<alias>]`, using that alias's `host`/`user`/`port`/
  `identity_file` fields exactly as `ai c -R -m <alias>` already resolves them (reuse the existing
  resolution helper rather than re-deriving it).
- `ai ssh` with no argument uses `[remote].default` (same default-resolution behavior as
  `ai c -R` with no `-m`).
- An unknown alias produces a clear error listing the configured aliases, not a stack trace.
- Both short and long forms for any new flags, per this repo's CLI convention (CLAUDE.md § CLI
  Conventions) — e.g. if a `--machine`/`-m` override is added instead of/alongside the positional
  arg, both forms must exist.
- Command is documented (--help text at minimum; a one-line mention in the relevant reference doc
  if one already catalogs `ai` subcommands).
- New regression test(s) covering: default-alias resolution, explicit-alias resolution, and the
  unknown-alias error path (mock the actual `ssh`/`os.execvp` call — do not make a real network
  connection in tests).
close_reason: Shipped: ai ssh [ALIAS] command, commit 4f133da on main. Reuses _config.get_remote_machine for host/user/port/identity_file resolution. 3 new regression tests (default alias, explicit alias, unknown alias, empty-host guard, Windows rejection). Full suite: 2570 passed, same 2 known xdist-only flakes as baseline.

title: Route ai sync's memory-conflict LLM merge through Codex first, Gemini as fallback
description:
## Original request (verbatim)

> why do we need gemini api key? just change the llm merge to be handled by codex instead. you can have gemini as a fallback. go ahead and add a /beads-task and cc task for that and set it to in progress and /implement that. and then do the ai sync resolve and make sure the memory is not over the 200 line budget or whatever the limit / recommendation limit is

## Task details

`_llm_merge_memory_conflict()` in src/ai_cli/sync.py (line ~1643) currently only tries Gemini
(via GOOGLE_API_KEY_TIER_1 / GEMINI_API_KEY + the google-genai SDK), returning None (falling back
to 'resolve manually') whenever no Gemini key is configured in the invoking shell. This blocked
`ai sync resolve` from auto-merging 2 conflicted ai-harness memory files today, even though this
fleet's standard delegation path (~/.claude/bin/cx) was available and didn't need any extra
credentials to be wired up.

Change: make Codex (via `cx mechanical` -- low effort, deterministic text-transform tier, matches
this fleet's own effort-ladder guidance for this exact kind of task) the PRIMARY merge path, with
the existing Gemini implementation kept as a fallback only when the Codex path is unavailable or
fails (mirrors the existing no-markers-left / empty-output / exception -> None contract so callers
don't need to change). Preserve the public function name/signature `_llm_merge_memory_conflict(conflict_content, filename) -> str | None` used at sync.py:1067 and sync.py:2354.

TDD: reproduce the current gap (no Gemini key -> None -> manual-resolve-required) as a regression
test, freeze it RED, implement the Codex-first path, verify GREEN, then re-run the existing Gemini
fallback tests to confirm they still pass unmodified in behavior.
close_reason: Implemented, tested (39 sync tests + 2551 full suite, ruff clean), deployed to Mac uv tool + Hetzner uv tool + aido venv via ai update, and verified end-to-end with a real (non-mocked) ai sync resolve run against live conflicts -- Codex successfully auto-merged both conflicted ai-harness memory files with no API key needed. That live run also surfaced a real data-corruption bug in the pre-existing marker-detection logic, root-caused and fixed as AI-CLI-0wmi in a follow-up commit.

title: test_process_probe SIGCONT/SIGKILL removal test fails on macOS Python 3.14 (psutil.resume() still calls signal.SIGCONT)
description: Pre-existing failure, unrelated to AI-CLI-209. Confirmed pre-existing at commit 5c986b0 (bare, no AI-CLI-209 changes applied): 'pytest tests/test_process_probe.py::test_given_no_sigkill_or_sigcont_when_a_process_is_ended_then_it_still_ends' fails with AttributeError: module 'signal' has no attribute 'SIGCONT' (also collection ERROR for SIGKILL deletion). The test monkeypatches signal.SIGCONT/signal.SIGKILL off the signal module to simulate a platform without them (e.g. Windows), but psutil.Process.resume() on this macOS/Python 3.14 host still unconditionally references signal.SIGCONT internally (POSIX branch), so removing the attribute crashes psutil itself rather than exercising process_probe.py's own no-SIGCONT/SIGKILL fallback path. Likely needs the test to patch at a narrower boundary (e.g. mock psutil.Process.resume/kill rather than deleting real signal module attributes), or account for the Python 3.14 psutil version behavior on this platform. Discovered while independently verifying AI-CLI-209 (Codex cx implement delegation) via full-suite pytest run in worktree .worktrees/ai-cli-1/AI-CLI-209-remote-preview-mismatch.
close_reason: Codex delegation reviewed field-by-field against source, verified locally (ruff+pytest all green), shipped via PRs #81-86 (squash-merged directly, no admin bypass needed post AI-CLI-sz10 ruleset fix)

title: Session reclamation is Linux-only (/proc) and hides unguarded SIGKILL/SIGCONT on Windows
description:
## Scope

Read-only portability scan of src/ai_cli/ following the direnv bootstrap (PR #50). Findings below are ordered by severity. Counts are from the scan, not estimates.

## F1 (HIGH, functional gap on 2 of 3 platforms) -- CC-session reclamation is Linux-only

main.py lines ~339-560 implement abandoned-Claude-Code-session detection and reclamation entirely against /proc:

- _proc_start_ticks reads field 22 of /proc/PID/stat
- _proc_state reads field 3
- _pid_has_ended treats absence of /proc/PID as the answer
- _reclaim_abandoned_cc_session gates on _proc_start_ticks(...) == recorded

macOS has no procfs, and neither does Windows. On both, these return None, so "identified" is always False and _reclaim_abandoned_cc_session ALWAYS returns False before doing anything. The feature silently never works off Linux -- no error, just a permanent no-op.

The fix is already the repo's own documented pattern: psutil is a hard dependency (pyproject dependencies), and config.py:28 says verbatim "Uses psutil for cross-platform correctness (Windows, macOS, Linux)". psutil exposes Process.create_time() and Process.status(), which cover both the identity check and the state check. session_adopt.py:182 already acknowledges the "where /proc does not exist" case, so the codebase is internally inconsistent on this point.

## F2 (MEDIUM, latent crash) -- signal.SIGCONT and signal.SIGKILL are unguarded

main.py:515 sends signal.SIGCONT and main.py:518 sends signal.SIGKILL. NEITHER EXISTS ON WINDOWS. Verified on the Windows interpreter in this checkout:

  SIGKILL False / SIGCONT False / SIGTERM True

Both would raise AttributeError. Currently unreachable only by accident: the /proc gate in F1 fails first and returns before _end_session_process is called. Fixing F1 without fixing F2 CONVERTS A SILENT NO-OP INTO A CRASH, so these two must be fixed together. Note the surrounding code already guards os.killpg/os.getpgid with hasattr(), so the omission is inconsistent rather than deliberate.

## F3 (LOW, non-ASCII in console output)

Printed user-facing strings elsewhere in the codebase contain em dashes and box-drawing characters. On a cp1252 Windows console these render as replacement characters. quota.py:27 reconfigures sys.stdout to UTF-8 on win32, but only stdout and only in that module -- stderr and other modules are unprotected. ruff config deliberately ignores RUF001/2/3 with the note "box-drawing/symbols in CLI output are intentional", so this is a decision to revisit, not an accidental lapse. direnv_setup.py (PR #50) is ASCII-only in all printed output as the reference pattern.

## Verified CLEAN (no action)

- macOS-only tools: 5 sites (osascript x3, ~/Library, Library/Application Support). All correctly guarded by sys.platform == "darwin" or are docstrings. iterm2.py:294, notifications.py:237, sync.py:103.
- os.getuid: guarded by a sys.platform == "win32" early return that uses ctypes.windll.shell32.IsUserAnAdmin() instead (main.py:698-705).
- os.killpg / os.getpgid: guarded by hasattr() (main.py:488).
- Path handling: pathlib throughout; ruff PTH is enabled in select, so os.path drift is linted.
- XDG dirs: config.py has explicit win32 branches for config/state/cache/data using APPDATA and LOCALAPPDATA.

## Out of scope for this issue

The 105 test failures + 158 errors on the Windows host are environmental, tracked separately in AI-CLI-windows-test-suite-failures-nvqt (pytest 0o700 DACL + broken domain trust; LongPathsEnabled=0). They are NOT caused by any finding above.

## Suggested sequencing

F1 and F2 together in one PR (psutil-backed process identity/state plus guarded signals), with tests that fake a non-Linux platform so the no-op is provably fixed rather than merely reachable. F3 separately, since it needs a decision on whether unicode CLI output stays.
close_reason: Closed

title: Windows test-suite failures are environmental: pytest 0o700 DACL + LongPathsEnabled=0
description:
## Summary

The ai-cli-utils suite reports 105 failures + 158 errors on the Windows host. Both classes were traced to MACHINE configuration, not repo defects. Identical counts reproduce on main with no local changes.

## Class 1 -- 105 failures: "Permission denied" when git creates a directory

pytest creates its temp tree with mode=0o700. CPython on Windows implements that as a *protected* DACL: inheritance disabled, ACEs for SYSTEM, Administrators, and OWNER RIGHTS only, with NO explicit ACE for the user. Directories git creates underneath therefore inherit no usable ACE, and Git for Windows' MSYS access check is denied.

Measured, isolated outside pytest entirely:

| Parent created by Python | git clone into nested subdir |
|---|---|
| mkdir(mode=0o700) | rc=128 "could not create leading directories ... Permission denied" |
| mkdir(mode=0o777) | rc=0 |

ACL dump confirms the mechanism:

- 0o700 gives SYSTEM:(OI)(CI)(F), Administrators:(OI)(CI)(F), OWNER RIGHTS:(OI)(CI)(F) -- inheritance broken, no user ACE
- 0o777 gives all (I) inherited entries, INCLUDING the user's own full-control ACE

Compounding factor: icacls reports "The trust relationship between this workstation and the primary domain failed", so the user SID no longer resolves and OWNER RIGHTS does not satisfy the check.

Remedies attempted and MEASURED INEFFECTIVE (do not retry):

1. conftest tmp_path.chmod(0o777) at setup -- Windows chmod only toggles FILE_ATTRIBUTE_READONLY and cannot rewrite a DACL. Written, measured, reverted rather than shipped.
2. icacls DIR /inheritance:e -- clone still rc=128
3. icacls DIR /grant *USER-SID:(OI)(CI)F -- grant returned rc=0, clone still rc=128

Likely real fix: repair the domain trust (rejoin the domain). This is an IT action.

## Class 2 -- 158 errors: WinError 3, the system cannot find the path specified

LongPathsEnabled = 0 in HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\FileSystem, and core.longpaths is unset in git. Deep pytest temp paths plus the slugified project-dir name (which must match Claude Code's own slugify, so it cannot be shortened in this repo) exceed MAX_PATH.

Candidate fix (needs admin):

1. set LongPathsEnabled = 1
2. git config --system core.longpaths true

## Why this is filed rather than fixed

Neither class is a defect in ai-cli-utils code, and the one in-repo workaround that looked plausible was measured not to work. Both need machine-level changes that are the operator's call. Until they are applied, the suite cannot be used as a clean gate on this host -- which is why PR #50 shipped with these failures explicitly documented as pre-existing.
close_reason: Closed

title: VS Code shows false merge conflicts on wt-ai-cli-1 worktree pull on acn-windows
description:
## Original request (verbatim)

> why does vs code keep saying there are merge conflicts when i try to pull down latest commits for ai-cli-1 worktree on this acn-windows machine. add a /beads-task and cc task for this and set it to in progress and then investigate root issue and /bug-fix. maybe there's some stale cache or something. i don see any uncommitted changes in that worktree so not sure what merge conflicts need to be resolved. when i clicked the button to resolve merge conflicts in the notification, nothing popped up.

## Task details

VS Code SCM shows "merge conflicts" on the wt-ai-cli-1 worktree when pulling, but:
- `git status` shows clean working tree
- No MERGE_HEAD or CHERRY_PICK_HEAD state files present
- Clicking "resolve conflicts" shows nothing

Root cause (measured): the local branch wt-ai-cli-1 has its upstream tracking target set to
`refs/heads/main` (not `refs/heads/wt-ai-cli-1`). VS Code's pull for the worktree therefore
merges origin/main into the branch, and when there's any divergence VS Code flags it as a
conflict even though git considers the tree clean. The `vscode-merge-base` config key written
by VS Code also points to `origin/main`.

Fix: set the correct upstream so wt-ai-cli-1 tracks origin/wt-ai-cli-1, then push the branch.

title: Windows CI matrix comprehensively broken -- ~100 test failures across nearly every test file, root cause unscoped
description:
The test-windows CI job (Python 3.11/3.12/3.13 on windows-latest) has been failing on every main run for 24+ hours (checked back 15 runs to 08-15 05:06Z, all red). This is not a small bug -- roughly 100 individual test failures span nearly every test file (test_cli.py, test_session.py, test_remote.py, test_iterm2.py, test_sync.py, test_quota.py, test_workspace.py, test_growthbook_launch_toggle.py, test_copier_update.py, test_bare_worktree.py, and more). Recurring patterns observed: POSIX-only stdlib attributes assumed present (os.getuid, os.ttyname missing on frozen Windows os module), path-separator mismatches (backslash vs forward-slash comparisons), UnicodeEncodeError/UnicodeDecodeError (cp1252/charmap default encoding vs UTF-8 assumptions), execvp/Popen mock call assertions failing (0 calls expected 1, suggesting a Windows-specific code path that never reaches the mocked call), and tmux-dependent tests failing (README documents tmux as explicitly unsupported on Windows, so these may need a skip guard rather than a fix). README claims Windows is a supported platform via MSYS2 + Git Bash, so this is a real, currently-unaddressed gap between that claim and CI reality -- not obviously a recent regression (need to confirm how long this job has been broken; may predate recent work entirely).

This issue is scoped as RESEARCH FIRST, not a blind fix attempt (Sergei's explicit call, 2026-08-16): investigate and categorize the ~100 failures into causal buckets (missing POSIX-API guards, path-separator bugs, encoding bugs, mock/assertion issues specific to Windows code paths, tests that should be platform-skipped like the tmux ones), estimate the scope/cost of a real fix for each bucket, and produce a short root-cause + scoping writeup (not a full fix) so a follow-up decision can be made: fix incrementally, mark test-windows as continue-on-error until fixed, or descope Windows support entirely if the gap turns out to be structural.
